title: Heat & thermodynamics
subtitle: Energy, temperature and the limits of thermal change
prerequisites: Mathematical toolkit, Classical mechanics. Local mathematical bridges are taught before use; advanced topics retain their stated prerequisites.

lessons.title: Which way will energy travel?
lessons.idea: Temperature predicts the direction of heat transfer, not how much energy an object contains.
body: Imagine two blocks touching inside an insulated box. If one is hotter, energy can cross their contact because of the temperature difference. That transfer is called heat. It stops having a preferred net direction when their temperatures become equal.

Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer between objects that can exchange heat. Molecules do not stop moving. A thermometer works by reaching this shared temperature, so a reading taken too quickly may still describe the thermometer changing.

equationGuide.meaning: A higher temperature drives spontaneous net heat transfer toward the lower temperature. The greater-than sign compares temperatures, not total stored energies.

check.prompt: A tiny hot bead touches a large cool block. Which claim follows before calculating heat capacities?
options: Net heat initially leaves the bead
The bead must contain more internal energy
Both must end at the arithmetic mean temperature
explanations: Correct. Direction follows the temperature difference, regardless of size.
Internal energy also depends on amount and material.
An arithmetic mean needs equal constant total heat capacities.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why can a metal spoon and wood feel different in the same room?
apply.answer: Touch senses how quickly energy leaves your skin. Different transport rates can feel different even at the same initial temperature; touch is not an equilibrium thermometer.

lessons.limits: Ordinary positive-temperature systems with thermal contact; work and chemical reactions are not inferred from this comparison.

glossary.definition: A connection that lets energy cross as heat.

lessons.title: A temperature value is not a temperature change
lessons.idea: Kelvin and Celsius have equal-sized steps but different zero points.
body: A rise from 20 degrees Celsius to 30 degrees Celsius is a rise of 10 degrees Celsius, also 10 kelvin. Converting an absolute temperature adds an offset; converting a temperature difference does not.
Absolute gas-law and engine ratios need kelvin. Write temperatures in kelvin before dividing them. The zero on the Celsius scale is not a zero of molecular thermal energy.

The numerical conversion between the scale origins ΔT: temperature change (K). Delta means final minus initial T_final, T_initial: endpoint temperatures (K). Final and initial identify the two readings

equationGuide.meaning: Add 273.15 to a Celsius reading to obtain its kelvin value; subtract endpoints to find a change.

apply.answer: A rise compares two states and could begin at many temperatures. A value of 10 K specifies one very cold absolute temperature. They share a unit but answer different questions.

lessons.title: Heat is a transfer, not a substance inside
lessons.idea: Internal energy belongs to a system; heat names one way energy crosses its boundary.
body: Choose a cup of water as the system. Its molecules have microscopic motion and interactions. Internal energy keeps track of that microscopic energy. We do not say the water stores heat, because heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference.

You can increase internal energy by heating the cup or by stirring it. Stirring transfers energy as work rather than heat. Equal internal-energy increases do not prove that the transfer mechanisms were the same.

equationGuide.meaning: Subtract the two stored internal energies; this change does not identify the path or the transfer mechanism.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Can a cooling sample have positive internal energy?
apply.answer: Yes. Cooling usually concerns a decrease, not the sign of an arbitrarily chosen energy reference. Compare changes and transfers, not an absolute zero chosen for bookkeeping.

lessons.limits: We separate thermal transfer from mechanical work; chemical and mass-transfer terms need additional accounting.

glossary.definition: Energy of microscopic motion and interactions inside the system.

lessons.title: A state is a snapshot, not the journey
lessons.idea: Equilibrium state variables describe a settled system without recording how it arrived.
body: A sealed gas can have a pressure, volume and temperature after it settles. Those numbers describe its state. The amount of heat used to reach that state describes a journey and is not another stored state variable.

A violently stirred gas may have different temperatures at different places. One temperature then hides important information. Before using a simple equilibrium equation, wait for settling or explain why a local-equilibrium approximation is reasonable.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Would the same final temperature guarantee the same state for any material?
apply.answer: No. Amount, volume, phase and composition can also matter. For an ideal fixed-composition gas internal energy depends only on temperature, but this special result is not a universal state description.

lessons.limits: Equilibrium descriptions and a fixed system; phase and composition must be specified when relevant.

glossary.definition: A quantity determined by the current equilibrium state.

lessons.title: Spread a push over an area
lessons.idea: Pressure measures normal force per area, not total force.
body: A gas pushes on each small part of a wall. When the push is uniform and perpendicular, divide total force by area to find pressure. Doubling the area at the same pressure doubles total force.

Use square metres for area. A centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, so a square centimetre is one ten-thousandth of a square metre. Confusing these conversions can make a pressure wrong by a large factor.
lessons.terms: p: pressure (Pa (pascal)). One pascal is one newton per square metre F: normal force magnitude (N (newton)). Only the perpendicular push is included A: contact area (m² (square metre)). Positive area, measured in square units

equationGuide.meaning: The same force spread over more area gives smaller pressure.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why do gas laws need absolute pressure rather than a gauge reading alone?
apply.answer: A gauge often reports pressure relative to the atmosphere. Molecules push even when gauge pressure is zero. Add the reference pressure before using an absolute-pressure state equation.

lessons.limits: Uniform normal stress; nonuniform stresses require adding contributions over the surface. Absolute and gauge references must not be mixed.

lessons.title: A mole is a counting bundle
lessons.idea: Amount of substance counts particles in very large bundles called moles.
body: Counting molecules one at a time is impractical. A mole is a fixed-size bundle, just as a dozen is a bundle of twelve. Unlike a dozen, a mole contains about six hundred thousand million million million particles.

Say what the particles are: atoms, molecules or specified ions. One mole of oxygen molecules is not one mole of oxygen atoms, because each ordinary oxygen molecule has two atoms. Amount in moles is not mass in kilograms.

apply.text: What must be clarified before converting one mole of a salt into a particle count?
apply.answer: Specify whether the counted entities are formula units, separate ions, or something else. The constant counts the selected entity; it does not decide the chemical description for you.

lessons.title: Connect a gas snapshot
lessons.idea: For an ideal gas, pressure times volume tracks amount times absolute temperature.
body: Imagine widely separated particles with negligible attraction and very small occupied volume. This ideal-gas model connects four state quantities. It does not say which variable stays fixed during a process; you must state that separately.

At fixed amount and temperature, a smaller volume means more frequent wall encounters per area and a larger pressure. Use absolute pressure and kelvin, and convert volume to cubic metres for the SI constant below.

The interactive curve may use litres and kilopascals: 1 L = 0.001 m³ and 1 kPa = 1000 Pa. Their factors cancel, so one kPa L equals one joule. Each curve fixes n and T; moving along it changes volume and absolute pressure. Changing n or T selects a different curve, not another point on the same isotherm.
lessons.terms: p: absolute pressure (Pa). One pascal equals one newton per square metre V: volume (m³ (cubic metre)). Space available to the gas n: amount (mol). Fixed unless particles enter or leave R: molar gas constant (J/(mol K)). Approximately 8.314462618 joules per mole per kelvin T: absolute temperature (K). Positive kelvin temperature; pV has units of joules

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why is doubling a Celsius reading not enough to predict doubled pressure?
apply.answer: Gas-law proportionality uses the absolute kelvin temperature. Doubling 20 °C to 40 °C changes 293.15 K to 313.15 K, not to twice its original value.

lessons.limits: Dilute equilibrium gas, negligible interactions and particle volume, no condensation. R is rounded for examples.

glossary.definition: A model that neglects particle volume and interactions except collisions.

lessons.title: Check whether the gas model fits
lessons.idea: A useful equation can fail when its simplifying assumptions fail.
body: Cooling a gas toward condensation lets attractions matter. Squeezing it tightly makes the particles’ own occupied volume matter. Both effects violate the simple ideal-gas picture, so success for a dilute warm gas is not permission to use it everywhere.
A measured ratio can test agreement with the model. A value near one supports the state equation for that state and precision; it does not prove that every other ideal-gas prediction is accurate.

Measured gas volume n: amount (mol). Known gas amount R: molar gas constant (J/(mol K)). Use consistent SI units T: absolute temperature (K). Positive equilibrium temperature

apply.title: Explain a new situation

apply.answer: Yes. Attractive and excluded-volume effects can partly offset. Agreement of one ratio alone is weaker evidence than agreement across several temperatures, densities and observables.

lessons.title: Still air is not still molecules
lessons.idea: Random molecular motion can remain large while average bulk velocity is zero.
body: A sealed gas can have no wind while its molecules fly in many directions. Velocities are signed or directed quantities, so opposite directions can cancel in an average. Speeds are nonnegative sizes and do not cancel that way.
Use a tiny toy sample to separate these ideas before considering a huge gas. The toy is not a full thermal distribution, but it makes the arithmetic distinction visible.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why should a thermometer not interpret a whole container moving past it as molecular temperature directly?
apply.answer: Temperature concerns random motion in the local rest frame, not bulk motion of the entire sample. First separate the sample’s shared drift from microscopic motion.

lessons.limits: Two-particle arithmetic is an illustration, not a thermodynamic equilibrium distribution.

lessons.title: Collisions make a steady push
lessons.idea: A wall feels force because collisions repeatedly change particle momentum.
body: A molecule bouncing off a wall reverses its perpendicular velocity. The wall supplies an impulse to change that momentum; the molecule gives the opposite impulse to the wall. Many tiny events create a nearly steady macroscopic force.
Divide total impulse delivered to a wall by elapsed time to find average force. Use the perpendicular velocity component, not the whole speed, when finding a bounce’s normal momentum change.

Positive observation interval

apply.answer: The incoming and outgoing velocities cancel in the bulk average, but each reversal transfers momentum to the wall in the same outward direction. The momentum flux does not vanish.

lessons.limits: Elastic reflection from a stationary massive wall; real collisions can exchange energy and need a broader model.

lessons.title: Temperature sets an average energy scale
lessons.idea: For a classical monatomic ideal gas, mean translational kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature.
body: A monatomic gas has single-atom particles. In the classical ideal-gas regime, random motion has three independent spatial directions. Each quadratic translational direction contributes half of the thermal energy scale on average.

This is an average over many particles, not an instruction that each particle has exactly the same energy. It describes translational motion and must not be applied to every possible internal degree of freedom at every temperature.

Exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin T: absolute temperature (K). Positive kelvin temperature 3/2: three halves (no unit). Three translational directions each contribute one half

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why can molecular rotation change heat capacity without changing this translational result?
apply.answer: Rotation adds another way to store energy when its levels are thermally accessible. The translational average can still hold while the total internal energy has extra contributions.

lessons.title: Square first, average second, then take a root
lessons.idea: Root-mean-square speed is not usually the ordinary mean speed.
body: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. To describe its average with one speed, first square each speed, average those squares, then take the nonnegative square root. The square root reverses squaring for a nonnegative input.

An actual equilibrium gas has a distribution of speeds: some slow, some fast. Its most common speed, average speed and root-mean-square speed answer different questions. Do not substitute one for another without checking the formula.

Picture a speed histogram: each bin counts the fraction of particles within a small speed interval. For the same particle mass, a hotter classical equilibrium gas has a broader distribution shifted toward higher typical speeds; it does not give every particle one shared speed. At the same temperature, heavier particles have lower characteristic speeds because the same average translational energy is shared with greater mass.

Square each speed before averaging √: nonnegative square root (no unit). The result whose square equals the input

Thermal bookkeeping often assumes the system is stationary and stays at the same height. If it speeds up or rises, include those changes too; do not label every energy change a temperature change.

The first law connects the two path-dependent quantities. It does not make either quantity into a state variable. A thermodynamic state is not a record of all heat previously supplied.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why must degeneracy be counted when comparing whole energy levels?
apply.answer: Several distinct microstates may share an energy. Each receives a weight; the total probability of that level includes all of them, not just one representative state.

lessons.limits: Canonical equilibrium, finite listed microstates, fixed particle number and positive temperature; energy-level degeneracies must be included explicitly.

lessons.title: The partition function is the normalization total
lessons.idea: Summing Boltzmann weights gives a compact way to organize finite-level thermal probabilities.
body: The partition function is the sum of the weights already introduced. It is not a probability and can exceed one. It depends on temperature and on the listed energy levels, including every distinct state.

If an energy level has several distinct states, multiply that level’s weight by its degeneracy when summing by levels. Use the same counting convention in the numerator when asking for a whole-level probability.

apply.answer: Omitted higher levels may acquire appreciable weight. A normalization over too small a list can then give misleading probabilities and energy averages.

lessons.title: Energy can change phase without changing temperature
lessons.idea: During idealized coexistence at fixed pressure, transferred heat can change the phase fraction instead of temperature.
body: At a fixed pressure, a pure material can melt while solid and liquid coexist at the melting temperature. Energy changes the microscopic arrangement and interactions, so temperature need not rise while the conversion continues.
Specific latent heat is energy per mass for the specified phase change and conditions. Heating before the transition, converting phase, and heating afterward are separate pieces of an energy account.

lessons.title: Choose the equilibrium rule that matches the constraints
lessons.idea: At fixed temperature and volume, Helmholtz free energy gives the equilibrium comparison for a closed system.
body: A system in a thermal environment can lower its own energy while also changing its entropy. Helmholtz free energy combines those two effects for fixed temperature, volume and particle number. It decreases in a spontaneous relaxation under those constraints and is minimized at stable equilibrium.

At fixed temperature and pressure instead, use Gibbs free energy, which also includes the pressure-volume term. The names are not interchangeable: first identify which environmental conditions are held fixed.

lessons.idea: Chemical potential measures how free energy changes when a small number of particles is added under stated constraints.
body: Two regions can exchange particles as well as heat. At the same temperature and pressure, moving particles can lower the combined Gibbs free energy when their chemical potentials differ. Equal chemical potential is the equilibrium condition for exchange of a given species.

The value is not simply the energy of one free particle. It includes how adding matter affects the whole thermodynamic state. We use a per-particle version in joules; chemistry often uses a per-mole version in joules per mole.

lessons.title: An average occupancy is not always a probability
lessons.idea: Mean occupation counts particles in a state and can exceed one when multiple occupancy is allowed.
body: Imagine repeatedly measuring how many particles occupy one specified single-particle state. For bosons, the outcomes can be zero, one, two or more. The weighted average count can therefore exceed one without any probability exceeding one.

For one fully specified fermion state, the Pauli rule permits only zero or one particle. In that special case, the mean count equals the probability that the state is occupied. Including an unresolved spin degeneracy would change what “one state” means.

At equality the ground-state expression diverges and needs separate limiting or condensate treatment. Fermi chemical potential may be above or below a state’s energy; its occupation remains between zero and one.

lessons.title: A zero-entropy limit needs a unique ground state
lessons.idea: The familiar zero-temperature entropy statement assumes a unique equilibrium ground state; unattainability is a distinct limitation.
body: As positive temperature approaches zero, excited states become less accessible in a system with a gap. If there is exactly one equilibrium ground state, the ideal statistical entropy tends to zero. If several ground states remain genuinely available, their degeneracy can leave a residual entropy.

This limiting statement is not a recipe for reaching absolute zero. The unattainability form of the third law says an ideal zero-temperature endpoint cannot be reached by a finite physical cooling procedure under its thermodynamic assumptions. Residual disorder in real materials also requires care about whether equilibrium was reached.

items.value: A model has one unique ground state, so g₀ = 1.

items.label: Reason
items.value: Its limiting entropy is k_B ln(1) = 0.

items.label: Conclude
items.value: A model with two equally accessible ground states instead has k_B ln(2), if that degeneracy persists and the equilibrium assumptions apply.

check.prompt: Does a zero limiting entropy for a perfect unique-ground-state model prove a finite refrigerator can reach exactly 0 K?
options: No, the limiting value and attainability are different claims
Yes, a limit is always reached after enough finite steps
Yes, because all motion must stop
explanations: Correct. A statement about approaching an endpoint does not provide a finite procedure to attain it.
Limits can be approached without being reached.
Quantum ground states can retain zero-point motion.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why should measured residual entropy not automatically be called a violation of the third law?
apply.answer: Ground-state degeneracy, frozen disorder or failure to reach equilibrium can matter. The zero-entropy version has assumptions, so investigate the state and preparation before claiming a contradiction.

lessons.limits: Equilibrium low-temperature counting with specified degeneracy; no full proof of the third law or realistic refrigeration design.

glossary.definition: A lowest-energy state of the specified system.
Entropy remaining in a low-temperature limit under the stated degeneracy or disorder conditions.

lessons.title: Draw the boundary before choosing the equation
lessons.idea: A thermal model starts by deciding what matter belongs to the system and what can cross its boundary.
body: A sealed piston gas, a kettle with escaping steam and a whole insulated room are different systems. The same event can appear as work entering one boundary and as internal conversion inside a larger boundary.

Begin with a written inventory: matter exchange, heat transfer, work, bulk motion and phase changes. Then select a balance that contains all the relevant terms. A familiar formula is not a substitute for this choice.
lessons.terms: ΔU: internal-energy change (J). For the fixed amount of matter inside the chosen system boundary Q: net heat into that system (J). Transfer caused by a temperature difference W_by: net work done by that system (J). Includes every counted work mode with the stated sign

options: Use an open-system account including energy carried by matter
Ignore escaped matter because it is invisible gas
explanations: The fixed-matter assumption is broken.
Correct. Matter crossing carries energy and requires additional accounting.
Gas is matter and its energy cannot be discarded.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: How does including an electric heater inside the boundary change the labels?
apply.answer: Electrical energy may cross the enlarged boundary as work and become internal energy inside it. If the heater is outside and only warms the gas through a wall, that gas boundary may receive heat instead. Total conservation remains consistent when boundaries are explicit.

lessons.limits: This lesson selects models, not a full open-flow derivation; unsafe thermal apparatus must not be built from these educational calculations.

glossary.definition: The chosen separation between what is modeled and its surroundings.

lessons.title: Use the state equation and energy balance for different jobs
lessons.idea: A gas state relation describes endpoints; the first law connects transfers along the process.
body: For a sealed ideal gas in a rigid container, the state equation predicts how pressure changes with kelvin temperature. The energy balance and heat capacity predict how much energy is needed to make that temperature change.
Keep these roles separate. The state equation alone does not tell you whether a temperature rise came from heat, stirring or electrical work. The supplied process conditions identify that.

Add 600 J of heat and no work: ΔT = 600/30 = 20 K, giving 320 K.

check.prompt: If the container leaks during heating, which assumption fails first in this calculation?
explanations: The temperature unit is unchanged.
Conservation still applies when all matter-carried energy is included.
Correct. The pressure ratio used n fixed, and escaping matter changes the energy account too.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: How would an unknown electrical input affect the inferred temperature rise?
apply.answer: The heat-only energy balance would omit a transfer. Include the electrical work with its sign before using heat capacity to infer temperature, then use the revised endpoint state in the pressure relation.

lessons.limits: Closed ideal gas, rigid volume, constant total C_V, no other work or phase change; equilibrium endpoints.

practice.prompt: A rigid sealed ideal gas starts at 250 K and 80000 Pa. C_V = 20 J/K; heat input is 1000 J with no work.
practice.reasoning: Energy balance determines temperature; the ideal-gas ratio then determines pressure. Entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not experimental uncertainty.

lessons.title: A proposed engine must pass two different tests
lessons.idea: Check both cycle energy conservation and the temperature-based entropy restriction.
body: A numerical engine claim may conserve energy and still violate the second law. First subtract rejected heat from absorbed heat and compare with the claimed work. Then compare its efficiency with the correct absolute-temperature bound.

Passing those two tests does not prove the detailed machine is buildable. It only removes two important contradictions under the stated reservoir model. Materials, rates and losses remain separate issues.

Use the same cycle quantities T_cold, T_hot: cold and hot reservoir temperatures (K). Strictly positive, with hot greater than cold ≤: at most (no unit). The reversible bound is an upper limit

steps: A claim uses 1000 J hot input, 600 J cold rejection and 400 J work between 500 K and 300 K.
Energy balances, and efficiency is 0.40.
The Carnot bound is also 0.40, so equality would require a fully reversible ideal engine, not ordinary finite-rate losses.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Why should a claim of performance above this bound prompt a search for omitted resources?
apply.answer: A hidden electrical input, chemical reaction or extra reservoir changes the model. Either the report is wrong or the two-reservoir heat-engine description is incomplete; neither conclusion should be concealed.

lessons.limits: Two fixed reservoirs and a complete cycle; no additional resource streams. Equality requires reversibility.

lessons.title: Report a thermal answer with its uncertainty and limits
lessons.idea: A final answer should show the model, units, plausible range and what could make it fail.
body: A well-insulated sample receives a measured heat amount with a stated range. If its heat capacity is known and constant, propagate that input range through the temperature-rise calculation. More calculator digits do not create more measurement precision.

Then perform an independent physical check: does the predicted state stay within the same phase and within the capacity’s valid range? A correct arithmetic result can still be a poor physical prediction when those assumptions fail.

Positive and treated as exact for this exercise T_final, T_initial: final and initial temperatures (K). Initial temperature is treated as exact here

options: Yes, only heater readings can be uncertain
No, capacity uncertainty must also be propagated
Yes, extra decimal places remove that uncertainty
explanations: Material properties can be uncertain too.

Printed precision is not measurement knowledge.

apply.title: Explain a new situation
apply.text: Give two ways the real final temperature could differ systematically from the simple prediction.
apply.answer: Heat leakage could reduce the net energy retained, and temperature-dependent capacity or a phase change could alter the relation between energy and temperature. These are model effects, not merely rounding errors; document and test them separately.

lessons.limits: Closed stationary sample, no work or phase change, constant known total capacity and exact initial temperature for this exercise. The ± range is a supplied bound, not automatically a statistical confidence interval.

glossary.definition: A stated range of plausible input or output values under a specified interpretation.
A repeatable bias or neglected process rather than random numerical rounding.

practice.reasoning: Use the same model at both input bounds and keep the uncertainty interpretation explicit. Entry tolerance permits rounding; it is not experimental uncertainty.
